steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement to bring in React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the ES6 import syntax to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react' here

// Your component will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have a valid import statement for React and useState.
successCriteria: The import statement must use the correct package name 'react' and import both React and useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import syntax. Make sure you're importing from 'react' and including both React and useState.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Remember to use `import React, { useState } from 'react';`.

steps.title: Import useEffect and useRef from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement to bring in useEffect and useRef from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the same import syntax as step 1, but with different named exports.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing hooks from 'react'
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have both useState and the new imports (useEffect, useRef) from 'react'.
successCriteria: The import statement includes both useEffect and useRef from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported useEffect and useRef. These hooks will be essential for managing side effects and storing mutable values in your WebSocket hook.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both useEffect and useRef from 'react' in a single import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import both useEffect and useRef from the 'react' package using the same syntax as the previous import.

steps.title: Create the useWebSocket custom hook function
steps.instruction: Create a custom hook function named 'useWebSocket' that takes a 'url' parameter (string) and returns an object. Place it after the imports.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts a URL parameter and returns an object. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A custom hook function named useWebSocket is defined with a url parameter and returns an object.
successCriteria: Function named useWebSocket
Accepts url parameter with string type
Returns an object
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the useWebSocket custom hook function with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named 'useWebSocket', accepts a 'url' parameter of type string, and returns an object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition doesn't match the requirements. Check that you've named it 'useWebSocket', included a 'url' parameter with type string, and made it return an object.

steps.title: Add TypeScript interface for the hook's return value
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface called UseWebSocketReturn that defines the shape of data returned by the useWebSocket hook. It should have three properties: sendMessage (function that takes a string and returns void), lastMessage (string or null), and readyState (number).
steps.hint: Define an interface above the useWebSocket function. Use the syntax: interface UseWebSocketReturn { ... } with appropriate type annotations for each property.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TypeScript interface named UseWebSocketReturn with three typed properties that will be used as the return type for the useWebSocket hook.
successCriteria: The interface must be named UseWebSocketReturn and include sendMessage: (message: string) => void, lastMessage: string | null, and readyState: number properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the TypeScript interface for the hook's return value. This provides type safety for the data structure that useWebSocket will return.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface has all three required properties with the correct TypeScript types: sendMessage should be a function that takes a string and returns void, lastMessage should be string | null, and readyState should be number.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to create an interface named UseWebSocketReturn with three properties: sendMessage (function), lastMessage (string or null), and readyState (number).

steps.title: Initialize state for lastMessage
steps.instruction: Inside the useWebSocket function, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'lastMessage'. Initialize it with null and specify its type as string | null.
steps.hint: Use useState with a generic type parameter to specify that lastMessage can be either a string or null.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a state variable for a message
const [lastMessage, setLastMessage] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The useWebSocket function now has a lastMessage state variable properly typed and initialized to null.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call inside useWebSocket that declares 'lastMessage' with type string | null, initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the lastMessage state variable. This will store the most recent message received from the WebSocket connection.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've properly typed lastMessage as string | null and initialized it to null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The lastMessage state variable wasn't properly initialized. Make sure to use useState with the correct type and initial value inside the useWebSocket function.

steps.title: Initialize state for readyState
steps.instruction: Inside the useWebSocket function, use the useState hook to create a state variable named readyState. Initialize it with the value WebSocket.CONNECTING.
steps.hint: Add a new useState call after the lastMessage state. Use the WebSocket.CONNECTING constant as the initial value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a state variable with a constant value
const [status, setStatus] = useState<number>(WebSocket.CONNECTING);
steps.expectedOutcome: The hook will have a readyState state variable initialized to track the WebSocket connection status.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call for readyState with WebSocket.CONNECTING as the initial value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the readyState state variable to track the WebSocket connection status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with WebSocket.CONNECTING as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The readyState state variable wasn't properly initialized. Try using useState with WebSocket.CONNECTING as the initial value.

steps.title: Create a ref to store the WebSocket instance
steps.instruction: Inside the useWebSocket function, create a ref using useRef to store the WebSocket instance. Initialize it with null and type it as WebSocket | null.
steps.hint: Use useRef<WebSocket | null>(null) to create a mutable reference that persists across re-renders.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a ref for a DOM element
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a socketRef variable that can hold the WebSocket instance without causing re-renders when updated.
successCriteria: The code must include a useRef call with the correct type annotation (WebSocket | null) and initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a ref to store the WebSocket instance. This ref will persist across re-renders and allow us to manage the WebSocket connection.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've typed the ref correctly as WebSocket | null and initialized it with null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ref wasn't created correctly. Remember to use useRef<WebSocket | null>(null) inside the useWebSocket function.

steps.title: Define the sendMessage function
steps.instruction: Inside your useWebSocket hook, define a function named sendMessage that takes a message parameter of type string and calls socketRef.current.send(message) if the WebSocket connection exists.
steps.hint: Create a function that checks if socketRef.current exists before calling its send method with the message parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The sendMessage function is defined and ready to be used to send messages through the WebSocket connection.
successCriteria: The sendMessage function should be defined inside the hook, accept a string parameter, check if socketRef.current exists, and call send() on it with the message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the sendMessage function. This function will allow components using your hook to send messages through the WebSocket connection.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your sendMessage function properly checks if socketRef.current exists before calling send(). Also verify it accepts a string parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sendMessage function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that takes a string parameter and uses socketRef.current.send() to send the message.

steps.title: Set up the useEffect hook for WebSocket connection
steps.instruction: Inside the useWebSocket function, create a useEffect hook that will handle the WebSocket connection lifecycle. The effect should run when the component mounts and clean up when it unmounts.
steps.hint: Use the useEffect hook you imported earlier. The effect function should create a new WebSocket instance and store it in the socketRef, then return a cleanup function that closes the connection.
steps.expectedOutcome: A useEffect hook is added to the useWebSocket function that will handle WebSocket connection setup and cleanup.
successCriteria: useEffect hook is declared inside useWebSocket
Effect function contains WebSocket creation logic
Effect returns a cleanup function that closes the WebSocket
Effect has an empty dependency array []
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the useEffect hook that will handle the WebSocket connection lifecycle. The empty dependency array ensures it runs only once when the component mounts, and the cleanup function will properly close the connection when the component unmounts.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track with the useEffect hook, but there are some missing elements. Make sure your effect function creates a WebSocket instance, stores it in socketRef, and returns a cleanup function that closes the connection. Also verify you have an empty dependency array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect hook for WebSocket connection isn't set up correctly. Remember to use the useEffect hook you imported earlier, create a new WebSocket instance inside it, store it in socketRef, and return a cleanup function. The effect should have an empty dependency array to run only on mount.

steps.title: Implement WebSocket event handlers inside useEffect
steps.instruction: Inside the useEffect hook, set up event handlers for the WebSocket's onopen, onmessage, onclose, and onerror events. Update the appropriate state values when these events occur.
steps.hint: Use socket.onopen, socket.onmessage, socket.onclose, and socket.onerror to assign handler functions. Remember to update state with setLastMessage for messages and setReadyState for connection status changes.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook will now have WebSocket event handlers that update state when connection events occur.
successCriteria: The useEffect hook should contain handlers for onopen, onmessage, onclose, and onerror events. The onmessage handler should call setLastMessage with the message data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up WebSocket event handlers. These will respond to connection events and update your hook's state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some event handlers, but make sure you have all four: onopen, onmessage, onclose, and onerror. Also verify that onmessage updates the lastMessage state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect hook doesn't contain the required WebSocket event handlers. You need to set up handlers for onopen, onmessage, onclose, and onerror events inside the useEffect.

steps.title: Add cleanup function in useEffect
steps.instruction: Inside the useEffect hook, return a cleanup function that closes the WebSocket connection stored in socketRef.current.
steps.hint: The cleanup function should check if socketRef.current exists and call its close() method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook now includes a cleanup function that properly closes the WebSocket connection when the component unmounts.
successCriteria: Return a cleanup function from useEffect
Check if socketRef.current exists
Call close() on the WebSocket instance
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've added a proper cleanup function that will close the WebSocket connection when the component unmounts, preventing memory leaks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your cleanup function checks if socketRef.current exists before calling close(). Also ensure you're returning the cleanup function from useEffect.
steps.feedbackWrong: The cleanup function is missing or incorrect. Remember to return a function from useEffect that closes the WebSocket connection stored in socketRef.current.

steps.title: Return the hook's interface object
steps.instruction: Complete the useWebSocket hook by returning an object with the sendMessage function, lastMessage state, and readyState state.
steps.hint: At the end of your hook function, use the return keyword followed by an object containing the three required properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useWebSocket hook should return an object containing sendMessage, lastMessage, and readyState, making these values available to any component that uses the hook.
successCriteria: Return statement at the end of the hook
Object with sendMessage property
Object with lastMessage property
Object with readyState property
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully completed the useWebSocket custom hook by returning all the necessary values and functions. The hook is now ready to be used in components to manage WebSocket connections.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning an object with all three required properties: sendMessage, lastMessage, and readyState. Check that you're using the correct variable names from your hook.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook isn't returning the expected values. Remember to add a return statement at the end of the useWebSocket function that provides an object with sendMessage, lastMessage, and readyState properties.
